newsitem.title: USA: Congress panel cool to Clinton U.N. dues plan.
newsitem.headline: Congress panel cool to Clinton U.N. dues plan.

text.p: An influential U.S. congressional subcommittee on Wednesday served notice that President Bill Clinton's proposal for a one-time appropriation to pay off nearly $1 billion in U.N. back dues was in trouble.

Members of the House of Representatives Appropriations subcommittee on state, justice and commerce said they would work with the administration to repay the arrears but objected to Clinton's plan to have Congress approve the funds now, before the United Nations made reforms.

In an odd twist for a Congress bent on cutting federal spending, committee members queried Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, on why she and the president did not seek more than a four percent increase for her department's 1998 operating budget.
"Obviously we would like more but we have to operate within a balanced budget," she replied.
The United States owes the United Nations more than $1 billion, mostly for peacekeeping missions, and officials say Washington's credibility with the world body has eroded because of this debt.

Moving to remedy the problem now that there is a new U.N. secretary general, Clinton in his 1998 budget request asked Congress for $100 million this year and a $921 million advance appropriation that would not be disbursed until 1999.

Albright said such a strategy was needed to persuade the United Nations Washington was indeed commited to pay its back dues. She said it would also maintain leverage over the organisation to carry out reforms because most of the money would not be paid out for more than one year.

But subcommittee chairman Republican Rep. Harold Rogers of Kentucky said the panel's preference was to consider a U.N. dues repayment programme whereby U.S. arrears would be voted by Congress one year at a time.
Democratic Rep. Alan Mollohan of West Virginia said of the Clinton proposal: "I have not heard much favourable comment about the idea ... So it might not be something that happens."
"The Lott initiative might be more realistic," he said, refering to Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott.

Officials said the Lott initiative involves a proposal for a high-level steering group including Albright and House and Senate leaders that would develop a plan to pay the arrears and make progress on U.N. reform.
